newsitem.title: USA: AGCO expects charge for Brazilian operation.
newsitem.headline: AGCO expects charge for Brazilian operation.

text.p: AGCO Corp said Thursday it expects to report non-recurring charges of between $5 million and $6 million during the current fiscal year as part of its efforts to cut costs at its struggling Brazilian operations.
Of that, $3.7 million was recorded in its third quarter.

The Brazilian operations, which were purchased by the company in June, have proved to be a drag on its third quarter results. That segment lowered the quarter's earnings by $3.3 million, or $0.06 per share, the company said.
Since acquiring the Brazilian operations, the company has sought ways to cut costs. So far, it said it has found about $15 million in savings that can be achieved by the end of the year.
Those measures include job cuts and product-cost reductions, it said. The company said it expects to eliminate the losses in the Brazilian operations by the end of the year.
AGCO also said it expects strong retail sales of equipment and a positive worldwide agricultural market to help its results in the near term.

Based on an anticipated successful harvest, coupled with high commodity prices and government subsidy payments to farmers, the company said it expects North American farmers will be encouraged to purchase equipment.

Uncertainties remain in the Western European agricultural market because of certain reforms and the effect of the so-called "mad cow disease," it said. However, farmers there have benefited from increased export demand and high commodity prices, the company said.
Overall, retail sales of AGCO's equipment in North America increased 20 percent during the first nine months compared with the same period in the prior year.
In Western Europe, overall retail sales for its equipment rose about nine percent over the same period in 1995.

Starting in the second half of 1995, the Brazilian agricultural equipment market dropped significantly because of the Central Bank's suspension of all loans for agricultural purposes under a special loan program, the company said.
Although those financing restrictions have since been resolved, the company said the suspension severely hurt farm equipment sales in 1996.
AGCO said it estimates that total industry tractor sales in Brazil in 1996 will be about 10,000 units, which falls under the five-year average of 20,000 units.
